card.keepWhy: Two words, everywhere he went, until they became him.
sources: Narada, the wandering sage and devotee of Vishnu, across the Puranas, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana; Bhagavata Purana 1.6.33 (he wanders the worlds playing his veena and singing of Hari)
Narada’s veena and his words “Narayana, Narayana,” as in popular tradition, films and storytelling
japa: repetition of a divine name or mantra; a mala traditionally has 108 beads
check: “Narayana, Narayana” as Narada’s constant words is a strong popular and theatrical tradition; confirm it is fine to present it as part of who he is in the stories, not as a scripture quote.

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there a good habit you keep starting and dropping? what if the habit were just one word?
options: then this sage is for you. listen.
then this one might stick. listen.
good. you’ll like him anyway. listen.

steps.line: Narada is the wandering sage of Hindu stories. He shows up everywhere: in heaven, on earth, in every kingdom.
He usually carries his veena, a stringed instrument.

steps.q: Besides his veena, Narada is famous in Hindu stories for something else. What?
o: Stirring up quarrels that end well
steps.why: He carries news, and gossip, between gods and kings, stirring trouble that turns out for the good. The Mahabharata’s scribe was Ganesha.

steps.q: Everywhere he goes, Narada says the same two words: “Narayana, Narayana.” What do you guess they are?
o: A name of God, said twice
A word for “peace,” as a greeting
steps.why: A name of Vishnu, one of his best-loved, said twice. Watch where he says it.

steps.line: And everywhere he goes, he says the same two words: Narayana, Narayana. A name of Vishnu.
He says it walking. He says it arriving. He says it leaving.

steps.q: Narada says it walking, arriving and leaving. Why does saying it everywhere matter?
o: So people will know he’s coming
Because the gods told him to
So it becomes part of who he is
steps.why: He doesn’t save it for a temple. Repeated all day, a name of God fills his whole life.

steps.line: It’s so much part of him that in Indian movies and cartoons, you know Narada has arrived when you hear it.
A tiny habit, repeated so often it became who he is. Hindus call it japa.
steps.label: japa

steps.q: Japa can be said aloud, whispered, or silently. Which does an old Sanskrit text rank highest?
steps.why: An old law book, the Manusmriti, says japa is worth ten times a ritual offering, whispered japa a hundred times, silent japa a thousand. Narada says it aloud, which is why everyone knows he’s near.

say: here’s what i love. narada never needed a retreat. he had two words, and he took them everywhere.
hindus call this japa: repeating a name of god or a mantra, often on a mala of 108 beads. said again and again, it slowly fills the heart.

steps.q: Narada isn’t a temple priest. He’s always on the road. From his story, what does that show about japa?
o: It belongs in a quiet temple
It only counts if others hear it
steps.why: Walking, arriving, leaving: Narada’s japa goes where he goes. A name of God can fill an ordinary day.

today.say: choose one word you love: a name of god like narayana or ram, or a word like peace. say it slowly ten times today, maybe while you walk, the way narada does. you can use a mala, or just your breath. it’s your choice.
options: “narayana” is narada’s. you can borrow it.
